analysis.one_liner: Makes public colleges tuition-free and cuts federal student loan interest rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote; after referral to a House subcommittee in March 2016, it went nowhere before the term ended, with only 3 House sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the federal government to give states grants, matched by state money, to eliminate tuition and required fees at public colleges. It also would have lowered interest rates on new federal student loans, let borrowers swap their existing loans to current lower rates, expanded the federal Work-Study program, and simplified the financial aid application. It never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at public colleges would gain the most: tuition and required fees would be eliminated, with states picking up roughly half the cost through matching funds. Borrowers with older, higher-rate federal loans could refinance to current lower rates, fixed for the life of the loan. Low- and middle-income students would benefit from expanded Work-Study funding aimed at the colleges serving the most Pell-eligible students, and from a simpler financial aid application that uses tax data from two years earlier.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public college students and loan borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Education Department to award states grants to eliminate tuition and required fees at public institutions, with each state providing matching funds equal to half the federal grant.

Sets lower interest rates for new federal student loans disbursed on or after July 1, 2016, and lets any borrower modify the rate on an outstanding federal loan to the current rate, fixed for the life of the loan.
Raises authorized federal Work-Study funding from $975 million in 2017 to $3 billion by 2021 and reallocates the money based on student need rather than each college's historical share.

Creates a pilot program letting students in five states file a single financial aid application for their whole degree program, and requires use of tax data from the second preceding year to ease the application.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the grant program, authorized at $47 billion for the first year and 'such sums as may be necessary' each year through 2026, with state governments covering the other half through matching funds. The federal government would also forgo interest income by letting borrowers refinance older loans to lower rates.

drawbacks.text: Authorizes $47 billion in federal spending for fiscal year 2017 and open-ended amounts each year through 2026, on top of a state matching requirement equal to half the federal grant.

Borrower refinancing to lower fixed rates would reduce the interest income the federal government collects on its student loan portfolio, a cost that would fall on the Treasury and, indirectly, taxpayers.

Conditions grants on states maintaining per-pupil instruction spending and ensuring at least 75 percent of instruction at public institutions is delivered by tenured or tenure-track faculty within five years, a federal requirement on how states run their university systems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to students are large and direct: free tuition at public colleges and cheaper loan repayment. The costs are also large and ongoing, with an open-ended federal authorization plus mandatory state matches, and the federal government gives up loan interest income through the refinancing provision. The bill's maintenance-of-effort rules try to keep the federal money from simply replacing state funding, but how much it would actually cost taxpayers depended entirely on future annual appropriations.

outcome.mechanism: The House Education and Workforce Committee never took the bill up; it was referred to a subcommittee in March 2016 and nothing further happened before the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Grayson (D-FL) introduced the bill on January 13, 2016, with two Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
On March 23, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training, where it remained.
No hearing, committee markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public-college students keep paying tuition and borrowers keep their existing loan rates; the federal budget avoids the multibillion-dollar annual cost and continues collecting current loan interest, while states avoid the matching-fund obligation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers and the federal loan portfolio

for.name: Two House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members signed on.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral, sent it to a subcommittee on March 23, 2016, and never held a markup or brought it to the floor before the term ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll call; all three House sponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-chaired committee where the bill sat took no action on it.

industries.industry: Federal student loan program and loan servicers
industries.note: Lower rates on new loans and a right for borrowers to refinance existing loans would reduce the interest collected on the federal loan portfolio and on the servicing contracts attached to it. Borrowers' gain is directly the portfolio's lost interest income.

States receiving grants would replace lost tuition revenue with federal-state funds, while requirements to maintain instruction spending, need-based aid, and tenure-track faculty share funding toward teaching rather than administration. Students gain the same money as free tuition.

Tuition-free public options would make tuition-charging private and for-profit schools less competitive for cost-conscious students, since the bill removes the price advantage of the cheapest alternative.
